cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.prompt: While you change 5-month-old Mia's diaper, she looks right at you and coos. Which response best supports her early language?

options.a: Smile, coo back, and pause so she can take a turn
options.b: Keep working quietly so she stays calm during the change
options.c: Name the colors on the wall poster to teach her new words
options.d: Play a recorded song so she hears plenty of language

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.explanation: This is serve-and-return: the infant sends a cue (cooing), and the caregiver answers it and then waits for the baby to respond again. These back-and-forth turns build attachment and the foundations of conversation, and routines like diapering are ideal times for them.

distractorExplanations.b: Staying silent misses the infant's bid for connection; diapering is a prime one-on-one time for talk, not a task to finish quietly.
distractorExplanations.c: Labeling poster colors ignores what Mia just did; language grows when the adult responds to the baby's own cue, not a new adult topic.
distractorExplanations.d: Recorded audio cannot respond to the baby; infants learn language from live, contingent exchanges with a caring adult.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.prompt: A 20-month-old points out the window and says, "Doggie run!" Which caregiver response best supports his language development?

options.a: "Say it the right way: The doggie is running."
options.b: "Good talking!" and then go back to the activity
options.c: "Yes, the big doggie is running so fast!"
options.d: "What color is the dog? What does a dog say?"

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.explanation: Expansion means repeating the toddler's idea and adding words and grammar ("the big doggie is running so fast"). It confirms the child was understood and models a slightly longer sentence without making him feel corrected, which keeps him eager to talk.

distractorExplanations.a: Correcting a toddler's grammar and asking for a repeat discourages talking; modeling the fuller sentence works better than correction.
distractorExplanations.b: Generic praise ends the exchange without adding any new words, so the child gets no richer language model to learn from.
distractorExplanations.d: Quizzing with test questions shifts away from the child's own idea about the running dog instead of building on what he said.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.prompt: A teacher sits beside a 2-year-old who is stacking blocks and says, "You put the red block on top. Now it's so tall!" Which language strategy is she using?

options.a: Self-talk, describing her own actions as she works
options.b: Open-ended questioning to stretch the child's thinking
options.c: Expansion, adding grammar to what the child just said
options.d: Parallel talk, describing what the child is doing

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.explanation: Parallel talk is narrating a child's actions as they happen ("You put the red block on top"). It gives words for exactly what the child is focused on, which is how toddlers connect new vocabulary to meaning without being asked to perform.

distractorExplanations.a: Self-talk is when adults narrate their own actions ("I'm pouring the milk"); here the teacher describes the child's actions.
distractorExplanations.b: The teacher makes statements and asks no question, so this is not open-ended questioning, which invites the child to explain or predict.
distractorExplanations.c: Expansion builds on words the child has spoken; this child said nothing, so the teacher is narrating, not expanding an utterance.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.prompt: During a small-group read-aloud, several 4-year-olds keep calling out comments about the pictures. Which approach best builds their language and comprehension?

options.a: Ask them to hold their comments until the story is finished
options.b: Pause to ask open questions and build on their comments
options.c: Read with lively voices so they stay focused on the words
options.d: Reread the book word for word until they can recite it

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.explanation: Interactive (dialogic) reading turns the child into a storyteller: the adult pauses, asks open-ended questions, and expands on children's comments. Research shows this builds vocabulary and comprehension more than reading straight through to a silent audience.

distractorExplanations.a: Saving comments for the end treats children's talk as a disruption and loses the moment when their interest and language are most active.
distractorExplanations.c: Expressive voices are helpful, but steering children back to listening only still keeps them passive instead of talking about the book.
distractorExplanations.d: Rote recitation builds memorized phrases, not the back-and-forth conversation and thinking that interactive reading develops.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.prompt: Ana, age 3, speaks Spanish at home and is just starting to use English in your family child care home. What is the best way to support her?

options.a: Use a few Spanish words and pair English with gestures
options.b: Ask her parents to use English at home so she learns it faster
options.c: Gently correct her each time she uses Spanish during play
options.d: Have her repeat English words in short daily drill sessions

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.explanation: Dual language learners do best when their home language is valued while English is built through meaningful context. Using a few familiar words from home and pairing English with gestures, pictures, and routines helps Ana feel secure and understand, and her home language skills transfer to English.

distractorExplanations.b: Asking families to drop the home language weakens the parent-child bond and the language base that later supports English learning.
distractorExplanations.c: Correcting her home language signals it is wrong, which can make her anxious and less willing to talk in any language.
distractorExplanations.d: Isolated word drills lack meaning and pressure the child; young learners pick up English through play, routines, and conversation.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.prompt: A preschool teacher wants children to begin recognizing printed words. Which classroom change does the most to support emergent literacy?

options.a: Post a printed alphabet chart high above the whiteboard
options.b: Add daily letter-tracing worksheets at the writing table
options.c: Label cubbies with names and shelves with words and pictures
options.d: Read a chapter book aloud to the group each day at rest time

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.explanation: A print-rich environment puts meaningful print at children's eye level where they use it every day. Seeing their own names on cubbies and word-and-picture labels on shelves teaches that print carries meaning, and name recognition is often a child's first reading.

distractorExplanations.a: A chart posted high up is out of children's line of sight and is not tied to daily use, so it does little to show that print has meaning.
distractorExplanations.b: Tracing worksheets practice letter forms out of context; preschoolers learn about print best through meaningful, hands-on use.
distractorExplanations.d: Reading aloud supports listening, but chapter books with few pictures at rest time do not help children notice and recognize print.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.prompt: A 4-year-old proudly shows you a painting he just finished. Which response best builds a healthy self-concept?

options.b: "That's the best painting in the whole class!"
options.c: Write his name on it for him so it looks neat
options.d: "You used lots of blue and filled the whole page!"

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.explanation: Specific encouragement describes what the child actually did, showing you truly looked and helping him value his own effort and choices. This builds self-concept from the inside rather than making him depend on adult judgments of "good" or "best."

distractorExplanations.a: Generic praise like "good job" is quick but vague; it judges the child rather than describing his work, so it teaches little about effort.
distractorExplanations.b: Comparing him with classmates turns art into a competition and can make children who are not "best" feel less capable.
distractorExplanations.c: Doing a task he could try himself sends the message that he is not capable; letting children write or attempt their names builds competence.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.prompt: Jaylen, age 3, drops to the floor crying when outdoor time ends. What should the caregiver do first?

options.a: Tell him calmly that crying won't change the schedule today
options.b: Stay close and say, "You're sad outside time is over."
options.c: Offer him a sticker if he stops crying and lines up
options.d: Ignore the crying so he learns it won't get him attention

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.explanation: Emotion coaching starts by staying near and naming the feeling. Labeling "sad" helps the child feel understood, calms the body, and gives him a word for the emotion; once he is calmer, the adult can help him cope and move on to the next activity.

distractorExplanations.a: Stating the schedule is accurate but skips the feeling; a child flooded with emotion cannot reason until he feels heard.
distractorExplanations.c: A sticker for stopping teaches that feelings should be hidden for a reward, and it gives him no skill for handling sadness next time.
distractorExplanations.d: Planned ignoring is for minor attention-seeking acts; a distressed young child needs an adult to help him regulate, not withdrawal.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.prompt: A toddler cries and clings to her father at drop-off every morning. What advice will best ease the separation over time?

options.a: Say a short, warm goodbye the same way each day, then leave
options.b: Slip out while she is busy playing so she does not get upset
options.c: Promise her a special treat at pickup if she does not cry
options.d: Stay and play with her for half an hour until she settles

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.explanation: A brief, predictable goodbye ritual (a hug, a wave at the window, "I'll be back after snack") lets the toddler learn that her parent leaves and reliably returns. The caregiver then helps her settle, which builds trust and shortens the crying over time.

distractorExplanations.b: Sneaking out may avoid tears today, but the child learns her parent can vanish without warning, which increases clinging and anxiety.
distractorExplanations.c: Rewards for not crying ask a toddler to hide normal feelings and do nothing to build the trust that makes separations easier.
distractorExplanations.d: A long goodbye stretches out the stress and delays the routine; a short, consistent exit is easier for toddlers to handle.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.prompt: Two 18-month-olds in an infant-toddler room both grab for the same push car. What is the most developmentally appropriate response?

options.a: Tell the child holding it to share and hand it over now
options.b: Explain that sharing is kind and ask them to take turns
options.c: Put the car on a high shelf so neither child can use it
options.d: Bring out a second car and name what each child wants

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.explanation: Toddlers are just learning that others have wants too and are not yet ready for true sharing. Offering duplicates of popular toys prevents many conflicts, and naming each child's wish ("You both want the car") builds the empathy and language that later make turn-taking possible.

distractorExplanations.a: Forcing a toddler to give up a toy teaches that bigger people take things; it does not build the understanding behind real sharing.
distractorExplanations.b: Explaining kindness and turn-taking is reasonable for preschoolers but expects more than 18-month-olds can understand or wait for.
distractorExplanations.c: Removing the toy punishes both children and gives them no words or strategies for the next time they want the same thing.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.prompt: Two 4-year-olds are pulling on the same shovel in the sandbox, both yelling "Mine!" The teacher calmly holds the shovel. What should she do next?

options.a: Give the shovel to the child who had it first and redirect the other
options.b: Set a timer and tell each child they will get two minutes
options.c: Ask each child what happened, then help them suggest solutions
options.d: Put the shovel away until both children can play nicely

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.explanation: Problem-solving steps are: calm everyone, hear each child and restate the problem, invite the children to suggest solutions, and help them pick one to try. Letting preschoolers generate the solution builds language, empathy, and conflict skills they can use without an adult.

distractorExplanations.a: Deciding who had it first ends the conflict but the adult does all the thinking, so the children practice no problem-solving.
distractorExplanations.b: A timer can be a good solution, but imposing it right away skips hearing the children and letting them come up with ideas.
distractorExplanations.d: Removing the shovel stops the tug-of-war but treats the conflict as misbehavior instead of a chance to teach negotiation.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.prompt: Children in a preschool room keep running between centers. Which statement is the best way to explain the safety rule to them?

options.a: "Walking feet inside keep our bodies safe from falls."
options.b: "Don't run inside, or you will have to sit out for a while."
options.c: "Stop running right now! Rules are rules in our classroom."
options.d: "Please be good and be careful when you're inside."

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.explanation: Rules work best when stated positively and with a reason. "Walking feet" tells children exactly what to do instead of what not to do, and "keep our bodies safe" explains why, which helps them remember and follow the rule on their own.

distractorExplanations.b: A "don't" rule names the unwanted behavior and adds a threat, but it never tells children what to do instead or why it matters.
distractorExplanations.c: "Rules are rules" gives no reason, so children learn to obey the adult rather than understand how running causes falls.
distractorExplanations.d: "Be good" and "be careful" are too vague for preschoolers; they need a specific action they can picture and do.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.prompt: During art, Leo, age 4, keeps painting on the table instead of his paper after one reminder. Which response is a logical consequence?

options.a: He loses outdoor time this afternoon for not listening
options.b: He helps wipe the table before he can paint again
options.c: He sits in time-out for four minutes, one per year of age
options.d: He gets no sticker on the behavior chart for the day

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.explanation: A logical consequence is directly related to the behavior, respectful, and reasonable. Cleaning the table he painted connects the action to its result, lets Leo repair the problem, and teaches responsibility instead of simply making him feel bad.

distractorExplanations.a: Losing outdoor time is unrelated to painting the table, so it is a punishment that does not teach Leo how to fix what happened.
distractorExplanations.c: Time-out by age removes him from learning and is not connected to the paint; it punishes rather than teaches the expected behavior.
distractorExplanations.d: Withholding a chart sticker is a reward system penalty, not a consequence tied to the mess, and it gives Leo no way to repair it.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.prompt: In a toddler room, Eli bites Zoe on the arm while they play at the sensory table. What should the caregiver do first?

options.a: Tell Eli firmly, "No biting!" and move him to a time-out chair
options.b: Have Eli say sorry and give Zoe a hug to make up right away
options.c: Call Eli's parents so they can talk with him about it today
options.d: Comfort Zoe and care for the bite, then tell Eli, "Biting hurts"

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.explanation: The bitten child comes first: comfort her and wash the bite with soap and water. Then give the biter calm, firm words ("Biting hurts") without a big reaction. Afterward, record when and where bites happen to spot patterns, and inform both families.

distractorExplanations.a: Time-out is not appropriate for toddlers, and focusing on the biter first leaves the hurt child waiting for comfort and first aid.
distractorExplanations.b: Forced apologies and hugs mean little to a toddler, and the bitten child may not want to be touched by the child who just bit her.
distractorExplanations.c: Families should be told, but a phone call is not the first step; the hurt child needs care and both toddlers need an adult present.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.prompt: A preschooler throws blocks almost every day at about 11:00. Before planning a response, what should the teacher do?

options.a: Remove the blocks from the room until the throwing has stopped
options.b: Ask his family which consequences they use at home
options.c: Record what happens before and after each throwing incident
options.d: Remind him of the block rule every morning at arrival

cda-childcare-readiness-check-social-com.explanation: An ABC observation (Antecedent, Behavior, Consequence) shows what triggers a recurring behavior and what keeps it going. The daily 11:00 timing hints at a cause such as hunger, a hard transition, or crowding, so data comes first and then a plan that prevents the trigger.

distractorExplanations.a: Removing the blocks takes away the materials but not the cause, so the behavior is likely to show up elsewhere at the same time.
distractorExplanations.b: Family input is valuable, but asking about home consequences assumes punishment is the answer before the trigger is understood.
distractorExplanations.d: A morning reminder comes hours before the problem and ignores whatever happens around 11:00 that sets off the throwing.
